div.head: The Lion
div.p: Therefore Jacob, blessing his son Judah, said: ‘A lion’s whelp is Judah, my son, of my own stock; who shall rouse him up?’
The Physiologus says the lion has three natures.

The first: when it walks in the mountains or the woods, and if it happens that it is sought by hunters and the hunter’s scent comes to its nose, at once with its tail it wipes out its tracks behind it, wherever it goes, so that no hunter, having followed its tracks, may catch it.

So too our Lord Jesus Christ, the spiritual lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, sent by the everlasting Father, covered over the intelligible tracks of his divinity, descending into the womb of the virgin to save the erring human race. And the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us. Therefore the powers of hell, not knowing that he had descended, said: ‘Who is this King of glory?’ The powers above answered, saying: ‘He himself is the Lord of hosts, and he is the King of glory.’
Of its second nature: when the lion sleeps, its eyes keep watch, remaining open;

as the bridegroom testifies of himself in the Song of Songs: ‘I sleep, but my heart watches.’ For indeed, in the flesh, the Lord’s body rested, but his divinity ever keeps watch at the right hand of the Father, according to that saying: ‘Behold, he who keeps Israel shall not slumber nor sleep.’

Of its third nature: when the lioness gives birth to her cub, she bears it dead, and watches over it for three days, until on the third day its father comes and breathes upon its face, and brings it to life.

So too God the almighty Father raised his Son our Lord on the third day from the dead, as Jacob had prophesied beforehand: ‘He shall lie down and rest like a lion, and like a lion’s whelp — who shall rouse him up?’

div.head: The Panther
div.p: There is also an animal called the panther, of varied color indeed, but exceedingly beautiful and very gentle. The Physiologus says that it is an enemy only to dragons. When it has eaten and filled itself with various prey, it withdraws into its den and, lying down, sleeps for three days. But rising from sleep, at once it sends forth a very deep roar, and together with the roar sends forth an odor of such great sweetness that this odor surpasses all spices and perfumes. When, therefore, all the beasts, whether near or far, hear its voice, they gather together and follow the exceeding sweetness of that odor. Only the dragon, when it hears its voice, hides itself in caverns underground; there, unable to bear the force of the odor, it grows numb, drawing itself together, and remains motionless and lifeless as if dead. But all the other animals follow the panther wherever it goes.

So too our Lord Jesus Christ, the true panther, drawing to himself, through his incarnation, the whole human race that had been taken captive by the devil and was liable to death, led captivity captive and gave gifts to men. For ‘panther’ is interpreted ‘taking all.’ So too almighty God, as we have said, seeing that the whole human race had been taken captive by demons and enslaved to idols, and that all peoples together had been made the devil’s prey, descended from heaven with the exceeding sweetness of his incarnation, and snatched us away; and we follow him, the Lord and the Lamb, wherever he goes. And the prophecy was fulfilled which says: ‘I have become as a panther to Ephraim, and as a lion to the house of Judah.’ By this it was already signified, at the time when Ephraim served idols, that the calling of the nations and of the people of the Jews was to be fulfilled through the coming of Christ. And because the panther is a many-colored animal, it signifies Christ, who is incomprehensible wisdom, wholly simple, wholly good, gentle and merciful, firm and steadfast, resplendent with manifold wisdom. For the panther is also a beautiful animal; so too Christ, as David says in the Spirit: ‘Fairer in form than the sons of men.’ It is also a gentle animal, as Isaiah says of Christ: ‘Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Zion, for your king comes to you, gentle, and bringing salvation.’ And because that animal, when it has eaten its fill, at once grows quiet and sleeps, so too our Lord Jesus Christ, after he had been filled with the mockeries of the Jews — that is, with scourges, blows, insults, reproaches, thorns, and spitting, and at last was hung upon the cross, fastened with nails, given gall and vinegar to drink, and pierced with a spear — sated with these gifts of the Jews, Christ slept and rested in the tomb; and descending into hell, he there bound the great dragon, the greatest and most ancient enemy of the human race. And that on the third day that animal, after its fill and its sleep, rises and sends forth a great roar, and a sweet odor breathes from its mouth, signifies that our Lord Jesus Christ, rising from the dead on the third day, fulfilled the prophecy written of him by David: ‘The Lord awoke as one out of sleep, like a mighty man that had been overcome with wine.’ At once he cried out, so that his voice was heard in all the earth, and his words to the ends of the world, saying: ‘Rejoice now, and do not be afraid; I have overcome the world.’ And again: ‘Father, those whom you gave me I have kept, and none of them is lost, save the son of perdition.’ And again: ‘I go to my Father and your Father, my God and your God; again I will come to you, and I will not leave you orphans.’ Likewise at the end of the gospel he said: ‘Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the world.’ And what can be sweeter or more pleasant than to breathe this odor — the odor of our Lord Jesus Christ — so that all who are near through faith and works, and those who are still burdened by weakness and are far off, may hear his voice, filled and refreshed with the most sweet odor of his commandments; and we seek him always, following him, crying out with the prophet: ‘How sweet are your words to my taste, O Lord, sweeter than honey to my mouth!’ And in the Song of Songs: ‘We run after the odor of your ointments; the maidens have loved you exceedingly.’ And a little after: ‘The king has brought me into his chamber; we will exult and rejoice in you.’ It behooves us, therefore, like young maidens — that is, souls renewed in Christ, and coming through baptism to newness of life — to run after the ointments of his commandments, that we may pass from earthly things to heavenly, and that the king may bring us into his palace, that is, into the heavenly Jerusalem, and there, exulting, we may say: ‘Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God’; ‘as we have heard, so have we seen, in the city of the Lord of hosts.’

div.head: The Unicorn
div.p: There is also another animal, called in Greek ‘monoceros,’ but in Latin ‘unicorn.’ The Physiologus says that the unicorn has this nature: it is a very small animal, like a kid, and has one very sharp horn upon its head, and no hunter is able to capture it. But they capture it by this device: they lead a virgin girl to the place where it dwells, and leave her there alone. And when it sees her, it leaps into the virgin’s lap and embraces her; and so it is caught, and is led away to the palace of the king.

So too our Lord Jesus Christ is the spiritual unicorn, of whom David says: ‘And my beloved is like the son of unicorns’; and again: ‘My horn shall be exalted like the horn of the unicorn.’ And Zechariah says: ‘He has raised up for us a horn of salvation in the house of David.’ And in Deuteronomy, Moses, blessing the tribe of Joseph, says thus: ‘His firstborn bull, majesty is his; his horns are the horns of a wild ox.’ That he has one horn signifies what Christ says: ‘I and the Father are one.’ The head of Christ is God. That he is called ‘very sharp’ means that neither principalities nor powers, nor thrones nor dominions, could understand him, nor could hell hold him fast. He is a very small animal because of the humility of his incarnation, as he himself says: ‘Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart’ — and yet he is so sharp that the subtlest devil is not able to understand or search out the mystery of his incarnation. But by the will of the Father alone he descended into the womb of the virgin, and the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us. And that the unicorn is said to be like a kid signifies the Savior who, as the apostle says, ‘was made in the likeness of sinful flesh,’ and condemned sin in the flesh.

div.head: The Hydrus
div.p: There is also another animal which lives in the river Nile, and is called the hydrus. The Physiologus says of it that this animal is a great enemy to the crocodile, and has this habitual nature: when it sees the crocodile sleeping on the riverbank with its mouth open, it goes and rolls itself in the mud, so that it may more easily slip into its jaws; and coming near, it leaps into the crocodile’s mouth, which at once swallows it alive. But the hydrus, tearing apart all its inward parts, comes forth alive from its belly, the crocodile now dead and all its inward parts torn asunder.

And this signifies death and hell, or every enemy of the Savior, who nevertheless, taking on our mortal flesh, descended into hell and tore apart all its inward parts, and led forth almost all who were held by it, devoured, in death, reproaching it, saying: ‘Where, O death, is your victory?’ And, according to the prophet: ‘O death, I will be your death; I will be your bite, O hell.’ For the bodies of many saints also rose with Christ at that time.

div.head: The Sirens and Onocentaurs
div.p: Of sirens and onocentaurs the prophet Isaiah speaks thus: ‘Sirens and demons shall dance in Babylon, and sirens and onocentaurs shall dwell in their houses.’

The Physiologus explains the form of each thus: sirens, he says, are deadly creatures, which from the head to the navel have the form of a woman; the remaining part, down to the feet, keeps the likeness of a bird, and they sing a certain most sweet melodious song,

by which sailing men are deceived, so that often, their hearing charmed and their senses beguiled, they are lulled to sleep; and then the sirens, seeing them thus asleep, fall upon them and tear their flesh to pieces. So likewise are deceived those who, delighted by devilish pomps and theatrical pleasures, or dissolved by musical tragedies, and, as it were, weighed down with sleep of mind, become the most eager prey of the adversary power.
In the same way the onocentaur is composed of two natures, as the Physiologus asserts. For its upper part is like a man, and its hinder part like an ass, and its nature is very savage.

By this are signified double-hearted and double-tongued men, of unformed character, having the appearance of godliness but denying its power, as the prophet David says: ‘And man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he is compared to the senseless beasts, and made like unto them.’

div.head: The Hyena
div.p: There is also another animal called in Greek ‘hyena,’ but in Latin ‘belua.’ Of it the Law says: ‘You shall not eat the hyena, nor anything like it.’ And it is said also through the prophet Isaiah: ‘The den of the hyena is my inheritance.’
The Physiologus relates of it that it has two natures: sometimes it is male, sometimes female, and therefore it is an unclean animal.

To it are compared the children of Israel, who at first worshiped the living God, but afterward, given over to luxury and pleasures, worshiped idols; or those who now are devoted to avarice, which is the service of idols, are compared to this beast. So too the unclean coot, which is said to be neither male nor female, that is, neither faithful nor faithless — but as Solomon says: ‘A double-hearted man is inconstant in all his ways.’

div.head: The Wild Ass
div.p: There is also another animal called the onager. The Physiologus says this of it: on the twenty-fifth day of the month Phamenoth, which is March, it brays twelve times in the night, and likewise in the day; and then it is known that it is the equinox, and that the days and nights are made equal in number of hours.

The wild ass bears the figure of the devil, who, knowing that the nights are made equal — that is, when he saw that the people of the nations, who walked in darkness, were turned to the perfect light, namely Christ — brays at every hour, day and night, seeking the food he has lost. Nor does it ever bray except when it seeks food, as Job says: ‘Does the wild ass bray when he has grass?’ — that is, unless it desires food. And the apostle says: ‘Be watchful, for your adversary the devil goes about as a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour.’ For as the ape has a head and no tail, and although it is a most disgraceful animal, yet in its hinder parts it is more disgraceful and horrible still; so too the devil had a head when he was an angel, an archangel, in the heavens, but because he was hypocritical and deceitful within, he lost it; he has neither head nor tail, because as he was cast down from heaven from the beginning and perished, so in the end he shall utterly perish, together with all who follow him — as also Paul, the herald of Christ, says of him: ‘Whom our Lord Jesus Christ shall slay with the breath of his mouth.’

div.head: The Elephant
div.p: Likewise there is a beast named the elephant. The Physiologus says of it that it has great intelligence in itself, but is said to have very little desire for mating. But at its proper time, when it wishes to beget offspring, it goes to the East with its mate, as far as the borders of paradise. There is in that place an herb called the mandrake, of whose fruit the female tastes first, and then leads the male to it, so that, persuaded, he too may eat. After both have eaten, they come together, and at once she conceives. And when the time of bringing forth draws near, she goes to a great pool and enters it up to her udders, and there gives birth in the water; and this she does because of the dragon, which lies in wait for her young and for herself. But the male does not leave his mate, but guards her over the pool of water as she gives birth, because of the serpent, which is the elephant’s enemy.

For these two elephants, male and female, bear the likeness of Adam and Eve, who were in the paradise of God before the transgression, surrounded by glory, knowing no desires of concupiscence nor the union of intercourse. But when the woman tasted of the forbidden tree, she gave to her husband, who, eating, was led astray. Then they were cast down from paradise into this world, as it were into a pool of many waters. That the waters signify the present age, because of its various troubles and pleasures, David suggests when he says: ‘Save me, O God, for the waters have come in even unto my soul.’ And elsewhere: ‘I waited patiently for the Lord, and he looked upon me, and drew me out of the pit of misery and the mire of the mud.’ When, therefore, they had gone forth into this pit of misery, Adam knew Eve his wife, and begot Cain in the mire of the mud. And so our merciful and compassionate Lord Jesus Christ, descending from the bosom of the Father, took our flesh, and drew us out of the pit of misery and the mire of the mud, and set our feet upon the rock. He put into our mouth a new song, saying: ‘Thus you shall pray: Our Father, who art in heaven,’ and so forth. This hymn he himself taught us, who set our feet upon the rock; and the rock was Christ, as the apostle says: ‘Now may the God of peace himself sanctify you wholly, that your whole spirit and soul and body may be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.’

Now I shall tell what the bones and hide of the elephant do. In whatever place or house they are burned, their odor at once drives away every serpent, or any venomous animal whatsoever, from that place. So likewise the commandments of God and works of piety, if they are kindled in the heart of man, put to flight every venomous work of the devil, in whatever part it may be.

div.head: The Antelope
div.p: There is also an animal named the antelope, exceedingly fierce, so that no hunter can approach it. For it has long horns, like a saw, with which it can cut down the greatest oaks. As it goes along it cuts down whatever thick and overhanging branches of trees it meets, yielding to nothing. But when it grows thirsty, it comes to the great river Euphrates and drinks. There are slender and pliant willow-shoots there. That animal begins to play with those shoots, and in playing entangles its horns; and being caught by both horns, it cries out with a roar, because, hemmed in by the slender shoots, it cannot escape. And then some hunter, hearing its voice from hiding, runs up, and finding it bound, kills it.

Concerning this, you too, who profess abstinence, trusting in your horns, ought to have cut away detraction, covetousness, and lust — that is, the worldly forest and the pomp of the devil — so that the angelic powers may rejoice with you. The two horns are the two Testaments; but do not play with wine, in which is excess, lest you entangle yourself and fall into the snare of the devil, who, seeing you hemmed in by vice, kills you. But the wise and prudent man turns himself away from wine and from woman.

div.head: The Saw-Fish
div.p: There is also an animal in the sea called the saw-fish, having very long spines near itself. And when it sees ships under sail, it swims to them, and raising its fins and tail, it sails like a ship, and strives to race against it. But when it has done this for a long time, it draws its fins back to itself, because, worn out by weariness and by the waves, it is carried back to its former place.

The sea signifies this world; the ships are the prophets and apostles, who passed through this world and overcame the adverse powers of this air. But the saw-fish, which could not persevere with the ships, signifies those who for a time profess abstinence, but do not persevere to the end with the saints, who, the sea overcome, arrive at the harbor of the heavenly homeland.

div.head: The Viper
div.p: Another example likewise was spoken to the Pharisees, setting forth a like matter: ‘Offspring of vipers, who has shown you to flee from the wrath to come?’

The Physiologus says this of the viper: when it mates, the male puts his mouth into the female’s, and she, swallowing his seed, bites off the male’s genitals, and he dies at once. Understand, then, what a harlot’s embrace does. But when the young have grown in the viper’s belly, they gnaw through and pierce her side, and so come forth, their mother dead.
Now the Pharisees are compared to vipers, serving shameful deeds and desires: they killed Christ their parent, and persecuted the Church, their mother.

div.head: The Serpent
div.p: Likewise in the gospel the Lord says: ‘Be wise, therefore, as serpents,’ and so forth.
The Physiologus says thus: serpents have three natures for doing harm.
The first:

when it grows old it suffers an impediment of its eyes, so that it cannot see. But see what it does: it fasts forty days and forty nights, until its skin is loosened; then it goes and seeks a cleft in a rock, and makes its way through it, and so is stripped of its skin and grows young again.
Narrow is the gate, and strait is the way, that leads to life.
The second nature of the dragon is this:
when it goes to drink, it first vomits out all its venom in its den or pit.

Let us also imitate this practice of the dragon: that when we come to drink water — that is, to hear the divine words in the church of God — we should not bring with us dusty and stained and worldly desires, but, our desires cleansed through humble and true confession, let us enter the temple of the Lord, praying and singing psalms to the Lord in our hearts.
The third nature of the dragon is this:
that when it sees a man naked, it flees from him in fear; but if it sees him clothed, it leaps upon him.
Let us also, being wise, understand that when our father was naked in paradise, the devil, the ancient serpent, did not prevail against him.

div.head: The Lizard
div.p: There is also a winged creature called the lizard, bright as the sun. The Physiologus says of it that when it grows old, both its eyes become clouded, so that it cannot even see the light of the sun. But it provides for its own nature a remedy of this kind: it seeks out a wall facing the rising sun, and going through a crack in it, with eyes opened, it is thus renewed by the light.

And you, O man, clothed in the old garment, when the eyes of your heart grow dim, seek a place of understanding; but turn yourself toward the East, and toward Christ our Lord, the sun of righteousness, whose name is called the Dayspring, that he may rise in your heart through the Holy Spirit, and show you the light of his mercy — he who enlightens every man that comes into this world.

div.head: The Stag
div.p: We read in the psalm: ‘As the hart desires the fountains of water,’ and so forth.

There are two kinds of stags. One kind, as soon as it finds a serpent in the cave where it lurks, breathes into it so that it comes out, and as it comes forth, striking it on the neck here and there, it kills the serpent and devours it. Afterward, because of the swelling, running to the purest waters, it vomits out the venom. But because of this it also changes its hair and casts off its horns; and it is even cast out by its fellows, until it is restored again.

This stag bears the figure of penitents, because penitents are constrained inwardly by the conscience of their sins, and go to the fountains — that is, to the teaching of the Scriptures — and are cast out, because through penance they separate themselves from the body and blood of Christ, until they are received back through the reconciliation of the priest. There is another kind of stag, which, if it finds a serpent, kills it, and after the victory seeks the mountain, where it may find pasture. So too every saint, when he perceives the devil pouring into himself or into others the venom of evil persuasion, strives with the Lord’s strength to slay it — that is, to cast it from himself — and comes to the mountain, that is, seeks Christ as the food of the soul.

div.head: The Roe
div.p: There is also an animal called in Greek ‘dorcon,’ but in Latin ‘caprea.’ Of this the Physiologus says that it loves high mountains and feeds in the valleys of the mountains. It is indeed a most excellent animal, foreseeing all things from very far away, so well that if it sees men walking in another region, it quickly recognizes whether they are hunters or travelers.

So too our Lord Jesus Christ loves the high mountains, that is, the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles, and all the saints. And as it is said in the Song of Songs: ‘Behold, my beloved comes like a roe’ — that is, our Lord Jesus Christ, who feeds in the Church through the works of piety which the faithful perform, as he says in his gospel: ‘I was hungry, and you gave me to eat,’ and the other praiseworthy things enumerated there. The valleys of the mountains figure the Church in her various places, as in the Song of Songs: ‘Turn, my beloved, and be like a roe or a young hart, upon the mountains of the valleys.’ Since, then, the roe has a very sharp keenness of eye, foreseeing from afar the snares of hunters, it signifies our Lord Jesus Christ, as Scripture says: ‘For the Lord is a God of knowledge.’ And elsewhere: ‘The Lord is high, and looks upon the lowly, and knows lofty things from afar’ — and as a most prudent provider of the creatures he has made, for the honor of his own name he looks upon, sees, and rules them; and before we fall into the devil’s snare, foreseeing with close attention, he shields us. But lest we be crushed by the darts of evil thoughts, he bids us seek the heights of the mountains — that is, to search out the meaning of the divine words — so that, as in a mirror, we may consider from them what pleases or displeases our Maker in ourselves. For as the roe sees the hunter, so our Lord Jesus Christ, foreseeing from afar Judas the traitor, said, as he had said: ‘One of you shall betray me’; and more plainly: ‘Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?’

div.head: The Fox
div.p: The fox is a most deceitful and treacherous animal. When it is hungry and finds nothing to eat, it seeks out red earth and rolls in it, so that it may appear thin and bloodied; and casting itself upon the ground, it lies as if dead, holding its breath within itself so that it may not seem to breathe outside. But birds, seeing it unwarily lying thus as if dead, come to it, and fly down and perch upon it. And the fox, perceiving this in silence, at once opens its mouth, seizes the bird, and eats it.

So without doubt the devil, and all heretics, whose likeness the fox bears, act toward all who live according to the flesh: they feign themselves as if dead, while holding them fast within the throat of their own power. Nor do they escape the devil’s throat, who are slaves to idleness and desires. For those who are occupied with the devil’s works are held bound by him, and are his portion, and shall be punished together with him, as the Lord says through the prophet: ‘They sought my soul in vain; they shall go into the lower parts of the earth; they shall be given over to the power of the sword; they shall be a portion for foxes. But the king shall rejoice, with all his saints.’

div.head: The Beaver
div.p: Likewise there is an animal called the beaver, a most gentle creature. For in medicine its testicles are said to be very useful against various ailments. The Physiologus has set forth its nature, saying that when it is tracked by a hunter, looking behind and seeing the hunter, it bites off its own testicles, and, casting them before the hunter’s face, flees. The hunter, gathering up the testicles, ceases to pursue it further. But if the hunter should overtake it suddenly, and, seeing that it cannot escape, it rears up and shows the hunter its genitals; and when he sees that it has no testicles, he lets it go.

So without doubt all who wish to live chastely in Christ should cut off from themselves all the vices of heart and body, and cast them before the face of the devil, and live in Christ. The apostle too admonishes us, saying: ‘Render to all their due: tribute to whom tribute is due, custom to whom custom, honor to whom honor.’ First let us render to the devil what is his — that is, renouncing him and all his works — and then at last, turned with our whole heart to God, let us render him, as to our Father, honor; and with his help let us shake off from ourselves the devil’s tax and tribute, and obtain spiritual fruits, that is, charity in good works, in alms, in visiting the sick, in the comfort of the poor, in praises of God and in constant prayers.

div.head: The Ant
div.p: Of the ant the Physiologus says that it has three natures.
Its first nature is this:

when it goes out from its hole, it walks in order, that is, each in its own rank. Those seeking grain carry each grain in their mouths into the hole. But other ants, empty-handed, meeting those who are carrying, take nothing away from their store along the way, but go on and gather their own food.

This the five foolish virgins did not do, who, taking no oil and going with empty lamps, said to the wise: ‘Give us of your oil, for our lamps are going out.’ But when the bridegroom came, the wise were let in, and the foolish were shut out.
Likewise its second nature.
When they store up grain in their hole, they split each grain down the middle, lest, moistened by damp, the grains sprout and they perish of hunger in the time of winter.

So too you, man of God, divide the Scriptures of the Old Testament into two parts, that is, between history and spiritual understanding, so that you may understand the truth. Separate the spiritual from the figure, and pass from the letter to the life-giving spirit, lest, the letter alone sprouting, you perish of hunger in the day of winter, that is, in the day of judgment. For the apostle says: ‘The law is spiritual, not carnal,’ and elsewhere: ‘The letter kills, but the spirit gives life.’ Likewise in another place: ‘Now these things happened to them as an example; but they were written for our sake, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.’ But the Jews, attending only to the letter and not having spiritual understanding, became the killers of their own Lord. Whence also they perish of hunger, because, busy with empty chaff, they lost the wheat. But you, man of God, strip the rods and remove their bark, as Jacob did, and, thus peeled, cast them into the waters, that your spiritual sheep may bring forth offspring — not carnal and vicious, but pure and uniform. These things are intelligible to spiritual men; but if you do not believe, you will not understand.
Likewise the third nature of the ant:

for when at harvest time they go out into the standing grain, by their own sense of smell they know whether it is barley or wheat in the field. If it is barley, it passes on to another ear and smells it; and if it perceives an ear of wheat, it climbs to the top of it, and, gathering the grain from it, carries it on its own shoulders to its own dwelling. For barley is the food of brute animals.

Flee, then, from barley, O man of God — that is, from the teaching of heretics. For barley-like things are to be cast away as filth, which destroy morals and kill the souls of men. Flee, then, Sabellius, and flee Marcion; flee Mani, beware of Novatian and Montanus; flee Valentinus, Basilides, Macedonius, Photinus, and the whole brood of Arius, all of whom scatter everywhere the stench of the dragon. The doctrines of all these are false and hostile to the truth.

div.head: The Hedgehog
div.p: The Physiologus says this of the hedgehog: the hedgehog has a certain likeness to a milky sphere, and is spiny on the outside. At the time of the grape harvest, it enters the vineyard, and where it sees a good bunch of grapes, it climbs up along the vine and strips off the grapes, so that they fall to the ground. Then, coming down, it rolls itself over the fallen grapes, so that it fills its spines with the grapes, and so carries food to its young.

You therefore, man of God, guard your vineyard diligently, and all its spiritual fruits; do not let the anxieties of this age and the pleasures of bodily vices occupy you, lest the spiny devil should perhaps scatter all your fruits, so that he may fix in your heart the stings of thorns, that is, of vices, and make you food for the beasts of the earth, and your vineyard remain bare and empty.
Fittingly, then, has the Physiologus set forth the natures of animals together with the understanding of the spiritual Scriptures.

div.head: The Eagle
div.p: David says in Psalm 102: ‘Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s.’

The Physiologus says the eagle has this nature: when it grows old, its wings become heavy and its eyes are clouded over with dimness. Then it seeks a fountain of living water, and flying up against the fountain, mounts on high, up to the fiery heat of the sun, and there burns its wings, and at the same time clears the dimness from its eyes. Then, coming down from the sun’s ray, it descends into the fountain, and plunges itself in three times, and at once it is renewed.

So too you, O man of God, whether Jew or Gentile, since you wear an old garment, and the eyes of your heart are dimmed, seek the spiritual understanding of the Lord, who said: ‘Unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.’ If, then, you are baptized of water and the Holy Spirit, then your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s. Likewise Saint Augustine discourses thus of the eagle, saying: when the eagle grows old, its upper beak grows so long that it is thereby hindered from eating. But going to a rock, it breaks it there, and so eats and lives as long as God wills. So too we are struck against the rock, that is, Christ. By the beak is understood the old garment which we put on from Adam. But we are renewed in baptism, and afterward we can receive the body of the Lord. Likewise Jerome relates that when the eagle grows old, it seeks the heights of heaven, that is, up to the fiery ether, and taking fire from it, burns its wings. And so, falling into its nest, it grows faint through its feathers, and its young feed it, until it is renewed. So too we, by the grace of the Holy Spirit, are burned, and meanwhile our vices and sins wither away, until we come in the age to come to everlasting renewal.

div.head: The Pelican
div.p: Of the pelican David says in Psalm 101: ‘I have become like the pelican in the wilderness.’

The Physiologus says of it that it is exceedingly fond of its young. But when it has brought forth its offspring and they begin to grow, they strike their parents in the face. The parents strike them back and kill their own young. But on the third day their mother, striking her own side, opens her breast and lies down upon her young, and pours out her blood over the bodies of the dead; and so, by her own blood, the dead young are restored to life and healed.

So too our Lord Jesus Christ, through the prophet Isaiah, says: ‘I have begotten and reared children, but they have despised me.’ Those, therefore, whom our Maker and Creator, almighty God, created, and made us to be when we were not, we, on the contrary, struck him in the face. And how do we not strike him, when in his very sight we serve the creature rather than the Creator? Therefore he deigned to ascend the cross, and, his side being pierced, blood and water came forth, for our salvation and eternal life.

div.head: The Night-Raven
div.p: In the same psalm David says: ‘I have become like a night-raven in the house.’
The night-raven is an unclean bird, and loves darkness more than light.

Therefore, gathering together, it signifies the Jews, who, when our Lord Jesus Christ came, drove his presence from themselves, saying: ‘We have no king but Caesar; but this man, we know not who he is.’ And therefore they loved darkness more than light; and for this reason the Lord deigned to turn to the Gentiles, and enlightened us who sat in darkness and in the region of the shadow of death; light has risen upon us. Of this people the Savior said through the prophet: ‘A people whom I have not known has served me.’ And elsewhere: ‘I will call those not my people, my people, and her not beloved, beloved.’ But of the Jewish people it is said, on the contrary: ‘The sons of the stranger have lied to me, and have limped away from their paths.’

div.head: The Coot
div.p: There is also a bird called the coot, very sagacious and most prudent above all the birds that fly over the earth. For it feeds on no carrion, nor does it fly or wander elsewhere, but remains in one place, and there, abiding to the end, has its food and rest in that same place, as David also says: ‘The house of the coot is their guide.’

So then every believer ought to act in this way: not to wander about seeking the food of heretics, nor to cling to worldly desires, like birds greedy for flesh; but always to remain in one place, that is, in the house of the catholic Church, with all purity, even to the end, and there to be fed not only with bread, but with every word of God.

div.head: The Partridge
div.p: There is likewise a bird called the partridge, exceedingly deceitful, as the Holy Spirit also says through the prophet Jeremiah: ‘The partridge has cried out, and has gathered what she did not lay; she makes herself riches unjustly. In the midst of her days they shall leave her, and at her end she shall be a fool.’

The Physiologus says the partridge is quite cunning, in that she steals the eggs of another partridge, which she then warms with her own body. But when the chicks are brought to the light and hear their mother’s voice, they leave the one who warmed them, and come to their true parents, moved, as it were, by a certain instinct of love; and the partridge by whom they were warmed remains, nonetheless, empty and foolish.

So too the devil, exceedingly deceitful, has attempted to seize for himself the creature formed by the Creator of all things in his own image; and having somehow seized those who lacked spiritual sense, he warmed them in various vices. But as soon as they heard the voice of the preacher, they returned to their true parents — to Christ, that is, and the Church — and there, embraced in eternal love, they are cherished, the foolish and empty devil left behind, robbed of his prey.

div.head: The Ostrich
div.p: There is also an animal called the ostrich, which the Greeks name struthiocamel, but the Latins call it a camel. Of this ostrich the prophet Jeremiah says: ‘And the stork in the heaven knows her time.’

The Physiologus says that it is a bird that does not fly, and has feet like a camel’s — for which reason the Greeks call it struthiocamel and the Latins camel. This animal does this: when the time comes for it to lay eggs, it lifts its eyes to heaven and gazes diligently at the stars called the Pleiades; and seeing them rising, it then lays its eggs. Of these stars Job also says: ‘Who made the Pleiades toward the south, and the constellations of the north, and the chambers of the south.’ For at that time — that is, when the crops flower and the heat is very great — these stars appear. Then the ostrich, seeing that the Pleiades have risen, digs in the earth and hides her eggs beneath the sand of that desert. But when she has gone away from that place, she forgets, and does not return to her eggs. For this animal is by nature forgetful, and so in the time of summer she lays her eggs and covers them with sand, so that what she herself ought to have done — that is, to sit upon her eggs and bring forth her chicks by her own warmth — the calm of that season and the mildness of the air seem to provide, so that, as soon as the sand, warmed by the heat, has baked the eggs, it hatches the chicks.

If, then, the ostrich knows her own time, and lifts up her eyes, and forgets her offspring, how much more ought we to recognize our own time? And lifting up the eyes of our heart, forgetting the things that are behind, let us press on, according to the apostle, toward the prize of the high calling. And the Lord says in the gospel: ‘He who loves father or mother, or brothers or sisters, wife or children, more than me, is not worthy of me.’ And elsewhere: ‘Let the dead bury their dead; but go and proclaim the kingdom of God.’

div.head: The Hoopoe
div.p: For it is written in the Law: ‘Honor your father and your mother,’ and so forth.

The Physiologus says: there is a bird called the hoopoe, whose young, when they see that their parents have grown old and, because of their dimness, can no longer see, lick their parents’ eyes and warm them beneath their wings, until they are restored to their former state;
and of what mind are those who do not render to their own parents the honor they owe?

div.head: The Caladrius
div.p: There is also a bird called the caladrius; it is written in Deuteronomy that it is not to be eaten. The Physiologus says of it that it is entirely white, having no part that is black. Its inward excrement cures dimness of the eyes. Whoever is held by sickness is usually known through this bird whether he is to live or to die. If, then, the sickness is unto death, at once the caladrius turns its face away from that man, and no one doubts that the man will die. But if he is to recover, the caladrius gazes intently at him, and, coming near, sets its mouth upon the man’s mouth, and by its breath draws out all the man’s sickness into itself; and then, flying into the paths of the sun, and casting off the sickness there, it scatters it, and the man is made whole.

So Christ too testifies of himself: ‘For the prince of this world has come, and has found nothing in me’ — he indeed who committed no sin, nor was guile found in his mouth. But coming to the sick people of the Jews, he turned himself away from them, and turned his face to our nations, taking away our sicknesses and bearing our sins, lifted up on the cross. Ascending on high, he led captivity captive and gave gifts to men. He came unto his own, and his own received him not; but as many as received him, to them he gave power to become the sons of God.

But if anyone doubts why unclean animals — such as the serpent, the dragon, the lion, and the eagle, and their like — are referred to signify Christ, let him know that sometimes they signify Christ’s strength and kingship, and sometimes, by their rapacity, they signify the devil.

div.head: The Phoenix
div.p: There is also a bird called the phoenix, whose figure our Lord Jesus Christ bears, who says in his gospel: ‘I have power to lay down my life, and power to take it again; no one takes it from me.’ Because of these words the Jews were enraged.

This bird is found in the regions of India. The Physiologus says of it that, when five hundred years of its life are completed, it enters into the wood of Lebanon, and fills both its wings with the various spices of that wood, making of various perfumes an enclosed nest, and gathers together a very great heap of twigs, placing its dwelling beneath. Then, approaching the heat of the sun, it draws fire to itself and kindles the twigs, and enters its nest in the month of Phamenoth — that is, March — and burns itself up; and the ash, on the first day, turns into a worm, on the second day into a fledgling bird, and on the third day it is restored to its former state.

This bird signifies Christ, both wings filled with a most sweet fragrance, that is, of the Old and New Testament. So too shall be the scribe in the kingdom of heaven, who brings forth from his treasury things both new and old.
